content: Muscle soreness, also known as delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), typically occurs after engaging in intense or unfamiliar exercise, particularly those involving eccentric muscle contractions where the muscle lengthens under tension. This soreness usually peaks between 24 and 72 hours after the exercise session. Many individuals consume antioxidant supplements or antioxidant-enriched foods before or after exercise, believing these interventions can prevent or alleviate muscle soreness. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects, both beneficial and harmful, of antioxidant supplements and antioxidant-enriched foods in preventing or reducing the severity and duration of DOMS. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated the effects of various forms of antioxidant supplementation, such as tablets, powders, concentrates, and antioxidant-enriched diets. Studies combining antioxidants with other supplements were excluded. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases and sources up to February 2017. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, assessed their risk of bias, and extracted data. The outcomes of interest included muscle soreness at various time points (up to 6 hours, 24, 48, 72, and 96 hours post-exercise), subjective recovery, and adverse effects. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 50 randomized, placebo-controlled trials were included, involving 1089 participants, of whom 88.2% were male and 11.8% were female. Participants ranged in age from 16 to 55 years and had varying levels of physical training, from sedentary to moderately trained. The studies were heterogeneous in terms of the timing, frequency, dose, duration, and type of antioxidant supplementation, as well as the type of exercise performed. All studies used antioxidant doses higher than the recommended daily allowance. However, many trials had significant methodological limitations, such as selective reporting and poorly described allocation concealment, which increased the risk of bias and potentially reduced the reliability of the findings. The review compared antioxidant supplementation to placebo but did not include comparisons between high-dose and low-dose supplementation within recommended levels. The pooled results showed a small reduction in muscle soreness with antioxidant supplementation at all main follow-up times. Specifically, the standardized mean differences (SMDs) were as follows: up to 6 hours (SMD -0.30), 24 hours (SMD -0.13), 48 hours (SMD -0.24), 72 hours (SMD -0.19), and 96 hours (SMD -0.05). However, when these results were rescaled to a 0 to 10 cm scale, the differences were minimal and unlikely to be clinically meaningful. For example, the mean differences (MDs) were -0.52 cm at 6 hours, -0.17 cm at 24 hours, -0.41 cm at 48 hours, -0.29 cm at 72 hours, and -0.03 cm at 96 hours. These values were all well below the minimal important difference of 1.4 cm. Subgroup analyses based on the type of DOMS-inducing exercise (mechanical versus whole-body aerobic) and funding source did not reveal any significant differences. Sensitivity analyses excluding cross-over trials showed no substantial impact on the results. None of the included trials measured subjective recovery, defined as the return to previous activities without signs or symptoms of DOMS. Adverse effects of antioxidant supplementation were reported in only nine trials involving 216 participants. Among these, two trials documented adverse effects. In one trial, all six participants in the antioxidant group experienced diarrhea, and four of them also reported mild indigestion, which are known side effects of the specific antioxidant used. In another trial, one out of 26 participants experienced mild gastrointestinal distress. In conclusion, the evidence from this review, which is of moderate to low quality, suggests that high-dose antioxidant supplementation does not lead to a clinically significant reduction in muscle soreness at any time point up to 96 hours post-exercise. There is no evidence available on subjective recovery, and only limited evidence exists regarding the adverse effects of antioxidant supplementation. These findings highlight the need for further research to clarify the role of antioxidants in managing DOMS and to establish priorities for future investigations in this area.
